title: Teacher Identity & Reflective Practice at Depth

pts: Teacher identity encompasses how a teacher understands their own role, values, and relationship to the profession — shaped by biography, training and experience.
This identity shapes classroom decisions often more powerfully than any single methodology or technique studied explicitly.
Two teachers trained identically can teach very differently based on how each has internalised the role.
points.who: Research on language teacher identity (e.g. Simon Borg's work on teacher cognition)

v: Paper; a set of metaphor prompts

items: Complete the sentence ‘A teacher is like a…’ with your own metaphor, and explain it in three lines.
Share metaphors in groups of four and note what each implies about the learner’s role.
Discuss where your metaphor came from: a teacher you remember, your training, your family?
Consider whether your metaphor fits your classroom on an ordinary day.
Keep the metaphor and revisit it at the end of the term.
DIET faculty collect metaphors from a trainee batch at the start and end of the course and compare them.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Metaphors from a teacher workshop in Tumakuru (written for this book):

lines: ‘A teacher is like a gardener. I water, but the plant grows by itself.’ Learner as active grower.
‘A teacher is like a pilot. I must bring everyone safely to the board exam.’ Learner as passenger.
‘A teacher is like a mother.’ Care and protection; possibly also control.

blocks.x: None is wrong. Each carries assumptions about who holds knowledge and who acts. Metaphor analysis is a widely used way of surfacing teacher beliefs.

body: Purpose: to show identity through metaphor. Content: four small panels: a gardener with a watering can, a pilot in a cockpit, a guide holding a lamp, a coach with a whistle; each with a caption about the learner’s role. Style: gentle, illustrative. Board version: four stick-figure sketches with captions.

items: Mentimeter (free plan) word cloud to collect metaphors anonymously.

blocks.x: Slips of paper collected in a box and read aloud.

pts: Teacher cognition studies the beliefs, knowledge and thinking that underlie observable classroom behaviour.
A teacher's tacit beliefs about how languages are learned often shape practice more than their stated, explicit methodology.
Surfacing these tacit beliefs — through reflection or action research (Unit 67) — makes them available for genuine examination.
points.who: Simon Borg's research on language teacher cognition

v: A belief questionnaire; a peer observer

items: Rate ten belief statements from 1 (disagree) to 5 (agree), e.g. ‘Learners should speak in pairs as much as possible’.
Choose two beliefs you rated highly.
A colleague observes one lesson and records evidence relevant to these two beliefs, for example learner talk time.
Compare the questionnaire with the observation notes.
Discuss any gaps without judgement: what pulled practice away from belief?
Use an audio recording instead of an observer, and time teacher and learner talk yourself.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A teacher’s comparison (written for this book):

lines: Belief rated 5: ‘Learners learn by speaking.’ Observed: teacher talk 31 minutes of 40; pair work 3 minutes.
Belief rated 4: ‘Errors are a natural part of learning.’ Observed: 14 immediate corrections during a fluency activity.

blocks.x: Teacher’s reflection: I believe in learner talk, but I am afraid of noise with 52 learners and of the head teacher passing by. Borg (2003) notes that contextual factors such as class size, examinations and school expectations often explain the gap between belief and practice. Naming the gap is the first step to closing it, or to revising the belief.

body: Figure 72.2 What I say, what I do

Purpose: to show the belief–practice gap. Content: a teacher’s speech bubble reading ‘Learners should talk!’ above a classroom where only the teacher speaks; a second panel after reflection shows pairs talking. Style: gentle humour, not mocking. Board version: two boxes, ‘Say’ and ‘Do’.

items: Google Forms (free) for the belief questionnaire; a phone stopwatch for timing talk.

blocks.x: A printed questionnaire and an observer’s tally sheet.

points.sub: Your own learning experience shapes your teaching
pts: A teacher's own experience learning languages often shapes their instincts about teaching, for better or worse, independent of current evidence.
Explicitly examining this influence — what worked or didn't for you personally, and whether it generalises — is a genuine reflective discipline.
This connects to Unit 25's principled eclecticism — personal instinct is one input to weigh, not an automatic authority.

items: Write 400–500 words on how you learned English: the teachers, materials, methods, successes and humiliations.
Underline three moments that still influence how you teach.
For each, ask: did this work for me because of the method, or despite it? Would it work for my learners?
Share one moment with a colleague.
Note one instinct you will keep and one you will now test.
Trainee teachers write the autobiography at the start of their course and revisit it at the end.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: In Class 8 our teacher made us learn fifty irregular verbs by heart and recite them standing. I was good at it and felt proud. Today I make my learners do the same.
Test: my learners can recite the verbs but do not use them when they write. My memory worked for me because I also read many English novels at home. Most of my learners do not have that.

blocks.x: Lortie’s (1975) apprenticeship of observation explains why such instincts feel natural. Personal experience is one valid input to weigh; it is not an automatic authority (Unit 25).

body: Purpose: to show biography shaping practice. Content: a teacher standing at a blackboard; behind her, a faint image of herself as a schoolgirl reciting verbs; a thread connects the two. Style: soft, reflective. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Docs (free) for a private autobiography that can be revisited.

blocks.x: A notebook kept as a reflective journal.

pts: Deeper reflection examines not just what worked, but why a teacher believed it would work, and what assumptions that belief rested on.
This extends Unit 9's practical reflective habit into more genuinely critical, identity-level reflection.
This level of reflection is more demanding and less immediately actionable, but often more transformative over a career.
points.who: Donald Schön's reflective practitioner, at its deeper "reflection on reflection-in-action" level

items: Choose a recurring problem, such as ‘Learners do not answer questions in English’.
Write your explanation of it and the assumption beneath that explanation.
Look through Brookfield’s (1995) lenses: your autobiography, learners’ views (a short anonymous survey), a colleague’s view, and what reading and research say.
Note which lens challenges your first assumption.
Rewrite the problem in a new way and plan one change.
Work through one lens a week for a month in a teacher circle.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Problem: My learners never volunteer answers.
First assumption: They are shy and weak in English.
Learners’ lens (survey): ‘If I answer wrongly, others laugh.’ ‘You ask and answer too quickly.’
Colleague’s lens: Your wait time is about one second.
Rewritten problem: My questioning routine gives no time to think and no safety for mistakes.

blocks.x: Reflection at this level asks why we believed something would work and what that belief rested on. It is harder and less immediately practical than ‘what worked today’, but often more transformative across a career.

body: Purpose: to show critical reflection from several angles. Content: a classroom scene viewed through four magnifying lenses labelled ‘Me’, ‘My learners’, ‘My colleagues’, ‘Research’; each lens reveals a different detail. Style: clear, symmetrical. Board version: a square divided into four with labels.

items: Google Forms (free) for an anonymous learner survey.

blocks.x: Learners write one honest sentence on a slip, unsigned, and drop it in a box.

body: Schön (1983) distinguished reflection-in-action, the quick adjustments made while teaching, from reflection-on-action, the later thinking back. Reflecting on your own reflection-in-action (why did I change course at that moment, and what did I assume?) is one route to the deeper level this unit describes.

pts: Research connects teacher beliefs about learner ability, language learning, and their own role directly to differences in classroom practice and outcomes.
This connects to Unit 22's self-efficacy research — a teacher's beliefs about learner capability can become a self-fulfilling influence.
Awareness of this connection is a genuine professional responsibility, not just abstract theoretical interest.

v: 30 minutes plus one week of observation

items: Without thinking long, mark each learner on your class list ‘high’, ‘middle’ or ‘low’ expected progress in English.
Over the next week, note for five learners from each group how often you call on them, how long you wait and what feedback you give.
Compare your treatment across the groups.
Choose one change, such as equal wait time or rotating names from sticks.
Repeat the tally two weeks later.
A peer observer records question distribution on a seating plan.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: ‘High’ learners: 23 questions, average wait 3 seconds, mostly open questions.
‘Low’ learners: 6 questions, average wait 1 second, mostly yes/no questions.

blocks.x: Rosenthal and Jacobson’s (1968) Pygmalion study suggested that teacher expectations can influence learner progress. Its methods have been criticized and later research shows smaller effects than first claimed, but the mechanism of different treatment is well documented. This connects to the learner self-efficacy discussed in Unit 22: what we believe about learners can become part of what they believe about themselves.

body: Purpose: to show how beliefs become outcomes. Content: a cycle: ‘Teacher expects less’ → ‘Fewer and easier questions’ → ‘Less practice’ → ‘Less progress’ → back to the start; a hand breaks the loop at ‘Fewer questions’. Style: clear cycle diagram. Board version: four words in a circle with arrows.

items: ClassDojo (free) random name picker, or any free random name generator.

blocks.x: Lolly sticks with learners’ names drawn from a jar.

pts: Teacher identity develops and shifts across a career, shaped by experience, further training, and changing professional contexts.
This connects to Unit 68's mentoring discussion — sustained professional relationships support this ongoing identity development.
A teacher's identity at year one and year twenty are rarely, and shouldn't be expected to be, identical.

items: Draw your career as a river, from first training to the present.
Mark bends (turning points), rapids (difficult periods), tributaries (people or courses that joined you) and calm stretches.
Beside each, write how your idea of yourself as a teacher changed.
Share with a mentor or peer (Unit 68).
Sketch where the river might go in the next five years.
Experienced teachers and trainees pair up to compare rivers across generations.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A river from a teacher with twenty-two years’ experience (written for this book):

lines: Year 1: new, rural Kannada-medium school; ‘I must look strict.’
Year 6: a Regional Institute course on communicative teaching; ‘I can make them talk.’
Year 12: became resource person for the block; ‘I teach teachers too.’
Year 20: mentoring young teachers; ‘My job is to ask good questions.’

blocks.x: Identity at year one and year twenty is rarely the same, and should not be. Sustained professional relationships, such as mentoring, support these changes.

body: Purpose: to show identity as developing across a career. Content: a winding river with labelled bends and tributaries, small figures of the teacher at different ages along its bank. Style: map-like, warm. Board version: a wavy line with labels.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) for a digital timeline.

pts: Institutional requirements sometimes conflict with a teacher's own pedagogical beliefs, requiring genuine, often difficult navigation.
This connects to Unit 25's practicality and possibility parameters — real institutional constraints shape what's actually achievable.
Honest acknowledgment of this tension, rather than pretending it doesn't exist, supports more sustainable long-term practice.

items: Read a case card, e.g. ‘You believe in process writing, but the school requires all notebooks corrected fully every week.’
Name the belief and the institutional requirement.
List what is fixed, what is negotiable and what is within your control.
Plan one honest, workable response.
Share and compare responses across groups.
Teachers write their own case cards from real experience, anonymized.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Fixed: weekly notebook check by the head teacher.
Negotiable: what ‘correction’ means. I propose coded correction (Unit 8) with learners doing the rewriting.
Within my control: a short note in each notebook explaining the code, so the check sees a system, not neglect.

blocks.x: Kumaravadivelu’s practicality and possibility parameters (Unit 25) recognize that real constraints shape what is achievable. Pretending there is no tension leads to frustration or cynicism; naming it honestly supports sustainable practice.

body: Purpose: to show agency within constraint. Content: three concentric circles labelled ‘Fixed’, ‘Negotiable’ and ‘Within my control’, with a teacher standing in the inner circle. Style: clean diagram. Board version: three circles with labels.

items: None needed; this is a discussion task.

points.h: Deep Reflection as a Practice, Not an Event
pts: Identity-level reflection benefits from sustained practice — a reflective journal, ongoing mentoring conversations — rather than a single occasional exercise.
This connects directly back to Unit 9's original reflective-practice habit, now extended to its deepest, most identity-engaged level.
This closes the individual-practitioner thread of Tier III before the tier's final posters turn to wider systemic questions.

items: Each week, write a short journal entry: one event, what you assumed, and what you now wonder.
Once a month, meet a reflection partner or mentor for thirty minutes to discuss one entry.
Each term, reread your entries and your teacher metaphor (point 1).
Write a half-page summary: what has changed in what I believe?
Use the summary to choose an action research question (Unit 67).
A DIET or cluster runs a monthly reflective circle, with rotating facilitators.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A weekly entry (written for this book):

lines: Event: Rahul answered in Hindi and I said ‘English, please’. He stopped talking.
Assumption: English-only produces more English.
Wonder: did it produce silence instead? (See Unit 71.)

blocks.x: Farrell (2015) argues for a framework in which reflection moves from practice to principles, theory and philosophy, and finally beyond the classroom. That can only happen over time. This closes the individual-practitioner thread of Part III; the next units turn to wider systemic questions.

body: Purpose: to show reflection as sustained growth. Content: a spiral staircase with journal pages on each step, labelled by term, rising towards a window. Style: calm, upward. Board version: a spiral drawn with dates.

items: Google Docs (free) or Microsoft OneNote (free) for a dated digital journal.

blocks.x: A notebook with a fixed weekly page layout.

body: For the next four weeks, write one journal entry a week using the pattern ‘Event, Assumption, Wonder’. At the end of the month, reread them together and underline one assumption that appears more than once.

dek: Unit 72 of 100: closing the individual-practitioner thread of this tier by examining how a teacher's own identity, beliefs and biography shape everyday classroom practice.

aims.x: Unit 9 introduced reflection as a practical habit: noticing what worked in a lesson and what to change. This unit goes deeper. It asks who is doing the reflecting, what they already believe, and where those beliefs came from. Two teachers can attend the same training and teach very differently the next Monday, because each brings a different history, set of beliefs and sense of what a teacher is. The unit is almost entirely for teachers, teacher educators and DIET faculty.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: define teacher identity and explain why it shapes classroom decisions;
explain teacher cognition and the gap between stated and enacted beliefs;
trace how your own experience as a language learner shapes your teaching instincts;
reflect at the level of assumptions, not only techniques;
recognize how beliefs about learners’ ability can influence outcomes;
map how your professional identity has changed across your career;
navigate honestly the tension between your beliefs and institutional demands;
build a sustained reflective practice rather than an occasional exercise.

why: Why this matters. Unit 9 introduced reflective practice as a habit. This poster asks what's actually being reflected on — the teacher's own formed identity and beliefs, not just technique.

background.x: Research on language teachers changed direction in the 1990s. Earlier work mainly observed what teachers did. Researchers then began to ask what teachers think, know and believe, and how this relates to what they do. Simon Borg (2003, 2006) called this field language teacher cognition and reviewed a large body of studies. A consistent finding is that teachers’ beliefs are powerful, often tacit, and resistant to change, and that what teachers say they believe does not always match what they do in class.

One source of these beliefs is long familiar. Dan Lortie (1975) called it the apprenticeship of observation: by the time we enter teacher education, we have already spent thousands of hours watching teachers. Many of our instincts come from that experience rather than from training. A teacher who learned English through translation and dictation in a Kannada-medium school in the 1980s, and succeeded, may feel in her bones that this is how English is learned, whatever her B.Ed. course said.

Teacher identity is a broader idea: how teachers understand themselves, their role and their place in the profession. Varghese and colleagues (2005) show that identity is not fixed but multiple, shifting and shaped by context, and that it is bound up with language itself, particularly for teachers for whom English is an additional language. Fred Korthagen (2004) placed identity and mission at the core of his ‘onion’ model, beneath competencies and behaviour. Donald Schön (1983) described reflection-in-action and reflection-on-action; Stephen Brookfield (1995) urged teachers to examine their assumptions through several ‘lenses’: their own autobiography, their learners’ eyes, their colleagues’ perceptions and the literature.

In India, NEP 2020 expects every teacher to take part in continuous professional development, suggesting at least fifty hours a year, and describes teachers as autonomous professionals (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). The National Curriculum Framework for Teacher Education had already called for reflective teacher education (NCTE 2009). Deep reflection is how that autonomy is used well. It connects with action research (Unit 67) and mentoring (Unit 68), and Unit 79 returns to teacher cognition as a research field.

items: Autobiography. A language-learning autobiography with three influences identified and evaluated.
Belief–practice comparison. A questionnaire and observation record, with a reflective commentary on any gap.
Critical reflection. A four-lens analysis of one recurring problem, with a rewritten problem statement.
Reflective portfolio. A term’s journal entries and a summary of changes in belief.
Which teacher from your schooldays do you most resemble in the classroom?
Which of your beliefs about language learning have you never tested?
Where does your practice differ most from your stated beliefs, and why?
Which learners do you expect least from? How might that show in your teaching?
How has your idea of yourself as a teacher changed in the last five years?
Who helps you reflect honestly, and how often do you meet?

perm: Teacher autobiographies quoted in the book must be original, fictionalized or used with written permission.

All metaphors, autobiographies, journal entries and tallies are original and written for this book. Screenshots of Mentimeter, Google Forms, ClassDojo, Canva or OneNote require permission or replacement with original illustrations. Real teachers’ reflective writing may be quoted only with their written permission.

terms.def: Lortie’s (1975) term for the many hours future teachers spend watching their own teachers as pupils, which shapes their beliefs about teaching before any training begins.
Reflection that goes beyond what worked to question the assumptions, values and wider social and institutional conditions behind teaching practice, and whose interests it serves.

The continuing learning and growth of teachers throughout their careers, through training, reflection, collaboration, observation and classroom research; it is most effective when sustained and linked to daily practice.

Thinking about and adjusting one’s practice while it is happening, such as changing an activity mid-lesson when learners are confused (Schön 1983). It contrasts with reflection-on-action, which takes place after the event.

Looking back on practice after the event in order to understand it and plan improvements, for example writing notes after a lesson or discussing it with a colleague (Schön 1983). It complements reflection-in-action.

A belief about teaching that a teacher holds without being fully aware of it, often formed through their own schooling. Such beliefs shape classroom decisions and can be surfaced through reflection, observation and discussion.
What teachers know, believe and think, and how this relates to what they do in the classroom (Borg 2003). It is shaped by schooling, training, experience and context.

The tendency for a teacher’s expectations of learners to influence their performance, through differences in attention, questioning and feedback (Rosenthal and Jacobson 1968). Low expectations of ‘weak’ learners can become self-fulfilling.

How teachers see themselves as professionals, shaped by their histories, language backgrounds, communities and work. For non-native-speaking teachers of English in India, a confident identity is an important professional resource.
